listed.name: Kevin Smith

source_evidence.quote:
Kevin Smith
Research Scientist
I am interested in how people use physical reasoning for a variety of common-sense tasks such as prediction, inferences about object properties, or action planning, and how to build this reasoning into AI. To support these capacities, we all have the ability to simulate how our environment will unfold based on the physics of the world. By using a combination of psychophysics and computational modeling, I study how we are able to perform this simulation, how we select between simulations and other forms of physical knowledge, and how we can draw on these predictions to make inferences about the world and plan our actions.

listed.name: Alex Alvarez

source_evidence.quote:
Alex Alvarez
Post-baccalaureate Student
How do minds generate, pursue, and revise goals across the vast space of all possibilities? How does our environment influence whether we exploit familiar goals or explore new ones? How can dysfunction in this exploration-exploitation tradeoff manifest as psychological disorders?
I’m interested in systems robust to deceptive rewards that sustain open-ended learning. I want to understand how minds avoid goals that appear valuable yet constrain exploration, and instead pursue unassuming goals that later scaffold cognitive structures and expand what can be imagined, learned, and pursued.

PhD Student
My research focuses on probabilistic 3D scene perception, with an emphasis on hierarchical, GPU-accelerated probabilistic modeling and inference for extracting robust structure from dynamic visual data. listed.name: Brian Leahy

source_evidence.quote:
Brian Leahy
Postdoc
I study the relationship between language and thought. I ask how features that may be universal and unique to human languages are related to the unique power of human thought. For example, every studies language has a way to flag a complete thought as merely possible (Maybe we’ll have tacos for dinner). Does learning to talk about mere possibilities support the development of cognitive apparatus that keeps track of the many ways the world might and might not be? I work with preschoolers, and have found striking differences in the algorithms preschoolers and adults use to make decisions when there are multiple open possibilities. I have also shown that learning to talk about possibilities is related to using adult algorithms in decision making.

Postdoc

listed.name: Katie Collins, PhD

source_evidence.quote:
Katie Collins, PhD
Postdoc
So much of individual and social life involves reasoning flexibly and efficiently about new systems of rules and reward, new games. How do people reason and create new games, alone and together? And how can we build more human-compatible AI systems that too can reason and efficiently about new systems — that meet our expectations and complement our limitations and, maybe, even warrant the label thought partner? I approach these questions (with amazing human thought partners!) by combining behavioral studies, computational modeling, and increasingly, ideas from game theory. I am passionate about building out an “applied” computational cognitive science that broadens the translational impact of CoCoSci as a field, putting computational cognitive science models to work in a range of fields (e.g., in medicine, mathematics, economics, psychiatry) and drawing on a wider range of real “systems” people engage in to improve, revise, and scale such models and inform new studies, broadening the range of rich human thinking that we can understand and empower.

listed.name: Marlene Berke

source_evidence.quote:
Marlene Berke
Postdoc
I study how we think about our own minds and other people’s minds. Even though we can’t directly see what’s going on in someone else’s mind, we often make pretty good inferences about what they might be thinking about, and even though we might never have broken our thumb, we might be able to make a pretty good inference about what that feels like. My work expands the scope of Theory of Mind inferences that our computational framework
can capture, going beyond mental states like beliefs and desires to mental processes like thinking and subjective experiences like pain.

listed.name: Matthias Hofer

source_evidence.quote:
Matthias Hofer
Postdoc
I am a postdoctoral scholar in MIT’s cocosci lab, prior to which I completed a PhD in the same department with Roger Levy. My research investigates the computational principles underlying how language and other symbol systems emerge and evolve through cultural transmission, and how their structure comes to reflect the cognitive, social, and cultural pressures under which they are learned and used. To explore these questions, I combine behavioral experiments with probabilistic modeling and tools from machine learning and information theory. A central theme of this work is that such systems are best understood as efficient programs, the product of a collective computation that converges, over generations, on solutions that are both expressive and easy to learn.

listed.name: Nitay Alon

source_evidence.quote:
Nitay Alon
Postdoc
Nitay Alon is a Rothschild Postdoctoral Fellow in the Computational Cognitive Science group at MIT, working with Josh Tenenbaum. His research asks how agents acquire and update their representation of the minds of others. Working at the intersection of cognitive science, AI, and economics, he studies Theory of Mind in mixed-motive multi-agent settings, including deception, skepticism, and over-mentalizing. His methods include probabilistic models and reinforcement learning. Nitay completed his PhD at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, jointly with the Max Planck Institute for Biological Cybernetics, under Jeff Rosenschein and Peter Dayan. His work has appeared in JAIR, Open Mind, and major AI conferences. He founded the ToM4AI community under AAAI, is editing a volume on Theory of Mind in AI, and is guest editor of a JAAMAS special issue on the topic.

listed.name: Sam Cheyette

source_evidence.quote:
Sam Cheyette
Postdoc
I’m a postdoc in the MIT cocosci lab interested in computational models of perception and learning. I did my graduate work with Steve Piantadosi at UC Berkeley. In one line of research, I have tried to understand the mechanisms underlying innate numerical cognition. Using behavioral experiments and computational models, I have tried to determine the link between the information people gather from the world to their ultimate perceptions of numerosity. I have shown that the psychophysics of number, including “subitizing” small numbers and Weber’s law for higher numbers, reflects optimal inference under a limited informational capacity. See an explainer here. Other interests include understanding constraints on concept-learning (e.g. simplicity, runtime complexity) and how people bootstrap complex algorithms from smaller pieces.

listed.name: Sam Hutchinson

source_evidence.quote:
Sam Hutchinson
PhD Student
I study how we make meaning from language. Beyond our ability to understand everyday speech, we’ve all had the experience of feeling our knowledge expand while reading a book or listening to a lecture—what is happening when we learn from language in this way? This caches out in two more targeted questions: where and how does our language system interface with our conceptual knowledge and semantic memory? What is the representational format of semantics in the mind and brain? I hope to make progress on these questions using techniques from computational cognitive science and cognitive neuroscience. I am also advised by Dr. Ev Fedorenko in MIT BCS.

listed.name: Zachary S. Siegel

source_evidence.quote:
Zachary S. Siegel
PhD Student
My research goal is to develop robots and AI systems that learn efficiently and generalize like humans — inferring goals, planning, and solving novel problems from limited data. Unlike neural systems that rely on large-scale imitation, I combine Bayesian inference with robot planning to enable flexible, adaptive behavior. I’m working on applying program induction to robotics, allowing robots to synthesize structured “programs” for tasks rather than fixed action sequences — improving generalization, reuse, and interpretability.

"value" : "This thesis considers four independent topics within linear algebra: determinantal point processes, extremal problems in spectral graph theory, force-directed layouts, and eigenvalue algorithms. For determinantal point processes (DPPs), we consider the classes of symmetric and signed DPPs, respectively, and in both cases connect the problem of learning the parameters of a DPP to a related matrix recovery problem. Next, we consider two conjectures in spectral graph theory regarding the spread of a graph, and resolve both. For force-directed layouts of graphs, we connect the layout of the boundary of a Tutte spring embedding to trace theorems from the theory of elliptic PDEs, and we provide a rigorous theoretical analysis of the popular Kamada-Kawai objective, proving hardness of approximation and structural results regarding optimal layouts, and providing a polynomial time randomized approximation scheme for low diameter graphs. Finally, we consider the Lanczos method for computing extremal eigenvalues of a symmetric matrix and produce new error estimates for this algorithm.",
